vignette:
Kofi, a 47-year-old park ranger, had spent years immersed in the beauty of nature, guiding hikers and monitoring wildlife. Yet, as he stood among the towering trees, he felt a gnawing tension in his chest that transformed the forest into a battleground of memories. His time as a civilian in a war zone haunted him-a place where fire and flames could erupt without warning, leaving behind chaos and destruction. Each reminder of that chaos, whether it was the crackle of dry leaves or the flicker of sunlight, propelled him towards drinking to numb the pain, as he believed that facing those memories directly would only expose him to further suffering. In moments of triggered panic, Kofi found himself reaching for alcohol as a means of escape, convinced that the only way to cope with the overwhelming memories was to dull his senses, further reinforcing his belief that he was unable to confront his trauma directly. Whenever the sound of crackling leaves or flickering sunlight triggered memories of his time in the war, he would instinctively reach for a drink, believing it was the only way to shut out the flood of emotions that threatened to engulf him. In those moments, Kofi felt an urgent need to numb the pain, believing that alcohol was his only means of coping with the overwhelming emotions that surged whenever he encountered those reminders. However, each time he chose to drink instead of facing his memories, it reinforced his narrative of being incapable of handling his struggles, leading him to further view himself as inadequate. The vivid images of those moments would creep into his mind, often triggered by the crackle of dry leaves or the flicker of sunlight through branches, making the serene environment feel threatening instead. Even the slightest criticism from a coworker could send him spiraling, reminding him of the harsh judgments he faced during the war, which had led him to believe that he wasn't good enough, that he had failed others. Each time he encountered criticism, he felt a wave of shame wash over him, reinforcing the belief that he was inadequate and unworthy, which magnified the feelings of threat he carried into every interaction. His conviction that he was inadequate made him hyper-aware of any critique, transforming constructive feedback into a perceived threat, as he increasingly felt that he had to defend against the judgments he dreaded. This negative appraisal of himself meant that even neutral comments could trigger intense feelings of threat, as he constantly anticipated criticism and rejection from others. This constant sense of inadequacy meant that even minor critiques would trigger a heightened response, causing him to brace for judgment and reinforcing his anxiety about how others perceived him. This constant anticipation of criticism heightened his sense of threat, leading him to believe that he was always on the verge of failure, which only fueled his need to withdraw and isolate himself further. His negative self-assessment created a lens through which he viewed the world as fraught with danger, making every social interaction seem like a potential minefield where he could fail. These triggers piled on top of one another, causing Kofi to cut off contact with friends and family, isolating himself in the belief that he was burdening them with his pain. This growing belief that he was a burden led him to feel that he had to keep his struggles hidden, which only served to heighten his awareness of potential criticisms from others, intensifying his sense of threat in social situations. His conviction that he was a burden made him hyper-vigilant, turning every social engagement into a potential minefield where he anticipated judgment and rejection, further igniting his anxiety. In choosing to isolate, Kofi felt he was reinforcing his belief that he was a burden, which only heightened his sense of threat whenever he thought about reconnecting with others.

Kofi's isolation deepened as he avoided anything that reminded him of the war, especially military uniforms and weapons. Whenever he encountered a police officer in uniform while on duty, a wave of panic washed over him, compelling him to retreat back into his solitary existence. He found solace in alcohol, using it as a crutch to numb the trauma, though he often awoke in a haze of guilt for having survived when so many others had perished. This guilt was an anchor, weighing him down and reinforcing his belief that he was somehow flawed; he felt he had violated his own values by not being able to protect those around him. It was the perfect storm, as his shame mixed with the threat of memories lurking just beneath the surface, leading him into restless nights where sleep became a distant memory. Even when he lay in bed, he felt a sense of danger that kept him alert and on edge, as if he were still waiting for an inevitable attack. This ongoing sense of threat was compounded by his avoidance behaviors; without confronting his fears, he never tested whether they were as justified as they felt, solidifying his belief that danger was ever-present. This persistent feeling of being in danger was reinforced by his avoidance behaviors, as he never allowed himself to test whether the threat was as real as it felt, solidifying his conviction that he could not truly relax or feel safe. His conviction that he was perpetually in danger meant that every sound, every flicker of light, became a potential signal of impending harm, making it impossible for him to find peace. This unrelenting sense of danger confirmed his belief that he was fundamentally flawed, leading him to feel that he was unworthy of safety or comfort in any situation. This relentless feeling of being in danger led Kofi to believe that he needed to be on guard at all times, reinforcing the idea that he could never truly relax or feel safe in any environment.

Each night, Kofi would replay the events in his mind, fueling his anxiety. In those dark hours, he found himself grappling with an overwhelming sense of threat that seeped into his daily life. When he experienced delays at work, such as waiting for equipment to arrive, he couldn't shake the feeling that something bad was about to happen. This constant state of vigilance only served to heighten his fears, making him more irritable and distrustful of the world around him. Every time Kofi found himself relying on alcohol to cope, he felt a quiet confirmation that he was incapable of facing his struggles without help, deepening his belief that he was fragile and unworthy. He felt trapped in a cycle where his triggers, threats, and negative appraisals reinforced one another. The guilt and isolation he felt only compounded his anxiety, convincing him that he was unworthy of connection or support. Each moment spent in isolation reinforced his belief that he was undeserving of compassion, further amplifying his sense of threat and vulnerability in any potential connection. This ongoing sense of unworthiness became a constant backdrop, heightening his feelings of vulnerability and confirming to him that he was undeserving of the help and support he craved. His belief that he was fundamentally flawed made him hyper-vigilant, as he interpreted others' reactions through this lens of unworthiness, leading to a heightened sense of threat whenever he found himself in social situations. This negative appraisal of himself meant that he was unable to engage freely with others, as he expected them to mirror his own feelings of inadequacy, which only served to heighten his anxiety and sense of threat.

As he navigated his days, Kofi's maladaptive strategies formed a protective shell around him, but it was a fragile one. He believed he was keeping himself safe by avoiding triggers, yet he was only deepening his sense of isolation and inadequacy. Each drink at night was an attempt to silence the memories, but it inevitably led to further isolation and a sense of failure for not facing his struggles head-on. The more he withdrew, the more he felt the weight of not living up to his values, reinforcing the notion that he was a coward for not confronting his past. Each avoidance further convinced him that he was weak for needing to escape his struggles, deepening his negative self-appraisal and convincing him that he was unworthy of facing the world without help. His avoidance of social situations and reminders of his trauma became a daily reminder of his perceived inadequacies, convincing him that he was incapable of facing the world without falling apart. Every time he chose to retreat into isolation, it validated his negative self-assessment, making him feel even more fragile and incapable, as if his need to avoid contact was proof of his inherent weakness. Each avoidance of social situations or reminders of his trauma fed into his negative self-appraisal, convincing him that his inability to cope was proof of a fundamental flaw within him. Each decision to isolate further deepened the cycle of negative appraisals about himself, making the triggers more potent.

Finally, the relentless grip of his symptoms became too much to bear. As Kofi sat with his growing distress, he became acutely aware that the very strategies he used to cope were only tightening the grip of his anxiety, making him feel increasingly trapped in a cycle of avoidance and fear. Each time he reached for alcohol to manage his distress, it confirmed his belief that he was incapable of facing his struggles without it, deepening the negative self-assessment that he was weak and fragile. Kofi realized that he could no longer manage this alone, especially as he felt himself slipping further away from the person he once was. Each use of alcohol to cope only served to reinforce his belief that he was weak and incapable, deepening his negative self-assessment and leaving him feeling more isolated than before. His hope for relief pushed him to seek help, but an underlying fear lingered-what if he could not face the truths that lay ahead? Would confronting his trauma render him even more vulnerable? As he prepared to take this first step towards healing, he clung to the hope that perhaps, through support, he might reclaim the solace that once filled his relationship with nature, transforming it from a hostile reminder into a source of peace once more. Yet, deep down, he feared that confronting his past might only serve as proof of his fragility, solidifying the negative beliefs he had come to accept about himself. This reliance on alcohol became a maladaptive strategy that reinforced his view of himself as weak, as he could not confront his trauma without it, further magnifying his feelings of inadequacy.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not establish that triggers lead to the use of maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals lead to the activation of triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not demonstrate that maladaptive strategies reinforce negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not indicate that maladaptive strategies contribute to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Kofi, a 47-year-old park ranger, had spent years immersed in the beauty of nature, guiding hikers and monitoring wildlife. Yet, as he stood among the towering trees, he felt a gnawing tension in his chest that transformed the forest into a battleground of memories. His time as a civilian in a war zone haunted him—a place where fire and flames could erupt without warning, leaving behind chaos and destruction. Each reminder of that chaos, whether it was the crackle of dry leaves or the flicker of sunlight, propelled him towards drinking to numb the pain, as he believed that facing those memories directly would only expose him to further suffering. In moments of triggered panic, Kofi found himself reaching for alcohol as a means of escape, convinced that the only way to cope with the overwhelming memories was to dull his senses, further reinforcing his belief that he was unable to confront his trauma directly. Whenever the sound of crackling leaves or flickering sunlight triggered memories of his time in the war, he would instinctively reach for a drink, believing it was the only way to shut out the flood of emotions that threatened to engulf him. The vivid images of those moments would creep into his mind, often triggered by the crackle of dry leaves or the flicker of sunlight through branches, making the serene environment feel threatening instead. Even the slightest criticism from a coworker could send him spiraling, reminding him of the harsh judgments he faced during the war, which had led him to believe that he wasn’t good enough, that he had failed others. Each time he encountered criticism, he felt a wave of shame wash over him, reinforcing the belief that he was inadequate and unworthy, which magnified the feelings of threat he carried into every interaction. His conviction that he was inadequate made him hyper-aware of any critique, transforming constructive feedback into a perceived threat, as he increasingly felt that he had to defend against the judgments he dreaded. This constant anticipation of criticism heightened his sense of threat, leading him to believe that he was always on the verge of failure, which only fueled his need to withdraw and isolate himself further. These triggers piled on top of one another, causing Kofi to cut off contact with friends and family, isolating himself in the belief that he was burdening them with his pain. This growing belief that he was a burden led him to feel that he had to keep his struggles hidden, which only served to heighten his awareness of potential criticisms from others, intensifying his sense of threat in social situations. His conviction that he was a burden made him hyper-vigilant, turning every social engagement into a potential minefield where he anticipated judgment and rejection, further igniting his anxiety. In choosing to isolate, Kofi felt he was reinforcing his belief that he was a burden, which only heightened his sense of threat whenever he thought about reconnecting with others.

Kofi’s isolation deepened as he avoided anything that reminded him of the war, especially military uniforms and weapons. Whenever he encountered a police officer in uniform while on duty, a wave of panic washed over him, compelling him to retreat back into his solitary existence. He found solace in alcohol, using it as a crutch to numb the trauma, though he often awoke in a haze of guilt for having survived when so many others had perished. This guilt was an anchor, weighing him down and reinforcing his belief that he was somehow flawed; he felt he had violated his own values by not being able to protect those around him. It was the perfect storm, as his shame mixed with the threat of memories lurking just beneath the surface, leading him into restless nights where sleep became a distant memory. Even when he lay in bed, he felt a sense of danger that kept him alert and on edge, as if he were still waiting for an inevitable attack. His conviction that he was perpetually in danger meant that every sound, every flicker of light, became a potential signal of impending harm, making it impossible for him to find peace. This unrelenting sense of danger confirmed his belief that he was fundamentally flawed, leading him to feel that he was unworthy of safety or comfort in any situation. This relentless feeling of being in danger led Kofi to believe that he needed to be on guard at all times, reinforcing the idea that he could never truly relax or feel safe in any environment.

Each night, Kofi would replay the events in his mind, fueling his anxiety. In those dark hours, he found himself grappling with an overwhelming sense of threat that seeped into his daily life. When he experienced delays at work, such as waiting for equipment to arrive, he couldn’t shake the feeling that something bad was about to happen. This constant state of vigilance only served to heighten his fears, making him more irritable and distrustful of the world around him. Every time Kofi found himself relying on alcohol to cope, he felt a quiet confirmation that he was incapable of facing his struggles without help, deepening his belief that he was fragile and unworthy. He felt trapped in a cycle where his triggers, threats, and negative appraisals reinforced one another. The guilt and isolation he felt only compounded his anxiety, convincing him that he was unworthy of connection or support. Each moment spent in isolation reinforced his belief that he was undeserving of compassion, further amplifying his sense of threat and vulnerability in any potential connection. This ongoing sense of unworthiness became a constant backdrop, heightening his feelings of vulnerability and confirming to him that he was undeserving of the help and support he craved.

As he navigated his days, Kofi’s maladaptive strategies formed a protective shell around him, but it was a fragile one. He believed he was keeping himself safe by avoiding triggers, yet he was only deepening his sense of isolation and inadequacy. Each drink at night was an attempt to silence the memories, but it inevitably led to further isolation and a sense of failure for not facing his struggles head-on. The more he withdrew, the more he felt the weight of not living up to his values, reinforcing the notion that he was a coward for not confronting his past. His avoidance of social situations and reminders of his trauma became a daily reminder of his perceived inadequacies, convincing him that he was incapable of facing the world without falling apart. Every time he chose to retreat into isolation, it validated his negative self-assessment, making him feel even more fragile and incapable, as if his need to avoid contact was proof of his inherent weakness. Each avoidance of social situations or reminders of his trauma fed into his negative self-appraisal, convincing him that his inability to cope was proof of a fundamental flaw within him. Each decision to isolate further deepened the cycle of negative appraisals about himself, making the triggers more potent.

Finally, the relentless grip of his symptoms became too much to bear. As Kofi sat with his growing distress, he became acutely aware that the very strategies he used to cope were only tightening the grip of his anxiety, making him feel increasingly trapped in a cycle of avoidance and fear. Kofi realized that he could no longer manage this alone, especially as he felt himself slipping further away from the person he once was. Each use of alcohol to cope only served to reinforce his belief that he was weak and incapable, deepening his negative self-assessment and leaving him feeling more isolated than before. His hope for relief pushed him to seek help, but an underlying fear lingered—what if he could not face the truths that lay ahead? Would confronting his trauma render him even more vulnerable? As he prepared to take this first step towards healing, he clung to the hope that perhaps, through support, he might reclaim the solace that once filled his relationship with nature, transforming it from a hostile reminder into a source of peace once more. Yet, deep down, he feared that confronting his past might only serve as proof of his fragility, solidifying the negative beliefs he had come to accept about himself.

This constant state of vigilance only served to heighten his fears, making him more irritable and distrustful of the world around him. Every time Kofi found himself relying on alcohol to cope, he felt a quiet confirmation that he was incapable of facing his struggles without help, deepening his belief that he was fragile and unworthy. He felt trapped in a cycle where his triggers, threats, and negative appraisals reinforced one another. The guilt and isolation he felt only compounded his anxiety, convincing him that he was unworthy of connection or support. Each moment spent in isolation reinforced his belief that he was undeserving of compassion, further amplifying his sense of threat and vulnerability in any potential connection. This ongoing sense of unworthiness became a constant backdrop, heightening his feelings of vulnerability and confirming to him that he was undeserving of the help and support he craved. His belief that he was fundamentally flawed made him hyper-vigilant, as he interpreted others' reactions through this lens of unworthiness, leading to a heightened sense of threat whenever he found himself in social situations. This negative appraisal of himself meant that he was unable to engage freely with others, as he expected them to mirror his own feelings of inadequacy, which only served to heighten his anxiety and sense of threat.

As he navigated his days, Kofi’s maladaptive strategies formed a protective shell around him, but it was a fragile one. He believed he was keeping himself safe by avoiding triggers, yet he was only deepening his sense of isolation and inadequacy. Each drink at night was an attempt to silence the memories, but it inevitably led to further isolation and a sense of failure for not facing his struggles head-on. The more he withdrew, the more he felt the weight of not living up to his values, reinforcing the notion that he was a coward for not confronting his past. Each avoidance further convinced him that he was weak for needing to escape his struggles, deepening his negative self-appraisal and convincing him that he was unworthy of facing the world without help. His avoidance of social situations and reminders of his trauma became a daily reminder of his perceived inadequacies, convincing him that he was incapable of facing the world without falling apart. Every time he chose to retreat into isolation, it validated his negative self-assessment, making him feel even more fragile and incapable, as if his need to avoid contact was proof of his inherent weakness. Each avoidance of social situations or reminders of his trauma fed into his negative self-appraisal, convincing him that his inability to cope was proof of a fundamental flaw within him. Each decision to isolate further deepened the cycle of negative appraisals about himself, making the triggers more potent.

Finally, the relentless grip of his symptoms became too much to bear. As Kofi sat with his growing distress, he became acutely aware that the very strategies he used to cope were only tightening the grip of his anxiety, making him feel increasingly trapped in a cycle of avoidance and fear. Each time he reached for alcohol to manage his distress, it confirmed his belief that he was incapable of facing his struggles without it, deepening the negative self-assessment that he was weak and fragile. As he prepared to take this first step towards healing, he clung to the hope that perhaps, through support, he might reclaim the solace that once filled his relationship with nature, transforming it from a hostile reminder into a source of peace once more. Yet, deep down, he feared that confronting his past might only serve as proof of his fragility, solidifying the negative beliefs he had come to accept about himself.
